item.title: Cells
item.description:
A cell is Go with statements allowed at the top level, as in a REPL:

import "strings"

func words(s string) []string { return strings.Fields(s) }

w := words("to be or not to be")
len(w) // the final expression is shown
$ notebook run words.md
── cell 0 (line 4, ran in 86µs)
 6

Declarations and statements

  • Top-level func, type and import are declarations of the notebook.
  • Everything else is a statement of the cell, run in order.
  • The names a cell defines at its top level — by :=, var, const, func or type — are notebook variables: every cell, and every function, can read them.

The final expression is shown

A cell’s final expression statement is its display value. A call with several results (fmt.Println’s n, err) is run for its effect and not shown.

A value with a Display() map[string][]byte method (the runtime.Displayer interface) shows itself: the map goes from a MIME type — text/plain, text/html, image/svg+xml, image/png, … — to the bytes of that representation. Values without one show their %v.

What a cell prints, through os.Stdout, the println builtin or C code, is captured and shown with it. (On systems without dup2 — Windows, js, wasip1 — os.Stdout and os.Stderr are swapped instead, and println is not captured.)

The three rules

They make the order of execution a function of the code, as in marimo, rather than of the order cells were run in.

One definition per name

Each notebook variable is defined by exactly one cell. Go already forbids two package-level declarations of a name, which gives this rule for free.

No assignment to another cell’s variable

A cell may not assign to a variable another cell defines: the dependency graph would not see the change.

```go
x := 1
```

```go
x = 2
```
$ notebook run rules.md
…
 error: 8:1: cell 1: cannot assign to x, which cell 0 defines; define a new name instead
notebook: 1 cell(s) failed

Mutation through a method or a slice element cannot be seen statically and is not refused (marimo makes the same choice).

Private names stay in their cell

A name starting with _, and err — which nearly every cell declares and none means to share — are local to their cell. Two cells may each have their own err.

Errors point at the notebook

The generated program carries //line directives, so compiler errors and panic stacks name the notebook’s own lines, not the generated file’s.

A cell that fails stops the cells that read it, and they say why:

```go
var xs []int
first := xs[0]
```

```go
first + 1
```
$ notebook run panic.md
── cell 0 (line 4, ran in 104µs)
 error: panic: runtime error: index out of range [0] with length 0
 …
 main._nbcell0(…)
 …/panic.md:5 +0x3c
 …
── cell 1 (line 9, kept)
 error: not run: cell 0 failed
notebook: 2 cell(s) failed

(The stack is shortened here; the frame of the cell names panic.md:5, the line of xs[0].)

Variables that cannot be shared

A notebook variable becomes a package-level variable of the generated program, which needs its type to be written there. A variable whose type cannot be written outside its package (an unexported type) cannot be shared: the error says so and suggests a private name (_x).

item.title: Ruby cells
item.description:
A ```ruby block is a Ruby cell (go-notebook v0.3.0 and later). The Ruby is rbgo, a Ruby bytecode VM written in Go, with the go-scikit bindings registered over the same Go libraries a Go cell imports:

Ruby Go library Counterpart
Stats go-statistics/stats scipy.stats
Special go-numerics/special scipy.special
Optimize go-numerics/optimize scipy.optimize
Integrate go-numerics/integrate scipy.integrate
DataFrame go-dataframe/dataframe pandas
Plot go-plot/plot matplotlib.pyplot
NDArray go-ndarray/ndarray (rbgo’s own) numpy.ndarray

Every binding calls the Go function it is named after; the bindings’ README lists every name.

The kernel adds github.com/go-scikit/ruby to the notebook’s work module by itself, and builds the worker with -tags rbgo_core (the Ruby language and its numeric stack, without gems). A notebook needs nothing more than go-notebook.

To try the same Ruby line by line, as irb, without a notebook file, run notebook irb.

A mixed notebook

A Go cell makes the data, a Ruby cell fits it with a go-scikit binding, and a Go cell reads the fit back (the file’s prose is left out here):

```go
xs := []float64{2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6, 4.4, 3.3, 2.8, 4.9}
```

```ruby
fit = Stats::Normal.fit(xs)
loc, scale = fit.loc, fit.scale
ks = Stats.ks_1samp(xs) { |x| fit.cdf(x) }
pvalue = ks.pvalue
fit
```

```go
import "fmt"

fmt.Printf("loc %.4f, scale %.4f, KS p-value %.4f\n", loc, scale, pvalue)
```

In a module whose go.mod has tool github.com/go-notebook/notebook/cmd/notebook and requires github.com/go-notebook/notebook v0.3.0:

$ go tool notebook run first.md
── cell 0 (line 6, ran in 0s)
── cell 1 (line 13, ran in 366µs)
 #<Stats::Normal loc=3.55, scale=1.2359207094308275>
── cell 2 (line 23, ran in 3µs)
 loc 3.5500, scale 1.2359, KS p-value 0.9381

In the Ruby cell xs is an Array of Floats; in the last Go cell loc, scale and pvalue are float64s. (A real transcript, from go-notebook v0.3.0 with go-scikit/ruby v0.1.0; the line numbers are those of the full file.) A larger example, with an NDArray and a plot, is examples/mixed.md.

The rules

Ruby cells follow the rules of Go cells: one definition per name, no assignment to another cell’s variable, and a name starting with _ stays in its cell. The names come from rbgo’s own parser: a cell defines the locals it assigns at its top level, and the methods, constants, classes and modules it defines there; it uses the names it reads before assigning them.

The Ruby cells share one interpreter, so their top-level locals persist from cell to cell. Dependencies, caching and re-runs work across the two languages as for Go alone: a Ruby cell runs again only when it, or a cell it reads, changed.

A cell that ends in an expression shows its value: a Plot figure as SVG, anything else as its inspect (an NDArray in NumPy’s form). An exception fails the cell with file:line: message (Class) at the notebook’s line, followed by the backtrace frames in the notebook (twelve at most).

How values cross between Go and Ruby

Only variables cross. A Go cell sees a Ruby cell’s top-level locals, not its methods, constants or classes, nor a local named like a Go keyword or predeclared identifier (len, type, int). A Ruby cell sees a Go cell’s variables, not its funcs or types.

Go to Ruby. Before a Ruby cell runs, each Go variable it reads becomes a Ruby local of the same name (a constant when the name starts with an upper-case letter):

  • numbers, strings and booleans as such;
  • slices as Arrays, maps as Hashes;
  • an *ndarray.Array as the NDArray itself, not a copy;
  • any other value (a *plot.Figure, a struct) as an object that comes back to Go as itself.

Ruby to Go. After a Ruby cell runs, each local it assigns becomes a Go variable whose type is the type of its value:

Ruby value Go type
nil any (nil)
true, false bool
Integer int64 (*big.Int when it does not fit)
Float float64
String string
Symbol ruby.Symbol
Complex complex128
Rational *big.Rat
NDArray *ndarray.Array, the same array
Array of all Floats, all Integers, all Strings, all booleans []float64, []int64, []string, []bool
any other Array []any
Hash with String keys map[string]any
Hash with Symbol keys map[ruby.Symbol]any
any other Hash map[any]any
a go-scikit object the Go value it wraps: *plot.Figure, stats.TTestResult, *optimize.Result, …
any other Ruby object ruby.Value, which a Go cell can Call

The type comes from the value, so it is known once the Ruby cell has run. A Go cell that reads a Ruby variable whose type is not known yet waits: the Ruby cell runs, then the Go cell is compiled with the type and runs, in the same run. When a later edit changes the type, only the Go cells that read the variable are compiled again.

Limits

A notebook is a program, and it runs with your rights. A Ruby cell can reach what a Go cell can: files through File, IO and Dir, other processes through Process, the environment through ENV, and the bindings that write files (DataFrame#write_csv, Plot::Figure#save_svg). The rbgo_core build leaves out the network libraries (socket, net/*, openssl): requiring one raises LoadError. Run only notebooks you trust.

Every cell runs in the worker, a process of its own, so the kernel survives whatever a cell does:

What the cell does What happens
runs too long with --timeout 30s, its worker is killed and the cell fails with “stopped: the cell ran longer than 30s”; the next run starts a new worker
holds too much memory with --memory 512 (MiB), the garbage collector keeps under the limit as long as it can, then the worker is stopped and the cell fails with “stopped: the cell went over its memory limit”
recurses without end Ruby raises SystemStackError, shown with twelve frames
asks for an impossible allocation ('x' * 2**62) Ruby raises NoMemoryError
calls exit or exit! a SystemExit fails the cell; the worker lives on
kills its own process (Process.kill, not on Windows; os.Exit in Go) the cell says so, and the next run restarts the worker

Both limits apply to Go and Ruby cells alike and are off by default. The memory limit counts the Go heap, sampled every 20 ms; memory held outside it (a large stack, a mapped file) is bounded only by the operating system.

In the browser

The playground runs Ruby cells too, with no server: the same rbgo and go-scikit bindings, compiled to WebAssembly. The page fetches the Ruby core (playground-ruby.wasm) only when the open notebook has a Ruby cell, so a visitor who runs only Go never downloads it. While the first core downloads, the page shows what go-notebook does, in cards that link to these pages; a core already in the browser’s cache opens the notebook without them. Each cell carries a badge, Go or Ruby, read from its fence (```go, ```ruby), never guessed from the code. The badge also says when the cell cannot run yet, for instance Ruby · loading the Ruby runtime…. A fence in another language stays prose and is marked not run: shown as text. Using the playground shows how to add a Ruby cell or switch a cell between Go and Ruby. The Ruby there has no bridge to the page’s JavaScript and no file system, and every figure a cell shows goes through an allowlist SVG sanitizer before it reaches the page. Try the Ruby examples on go-notebook’s own playground, go-statistics and go-numerics.

item.title: Julia cells
item.description:
A ```julia block is a Julia cell (parsed since go-notebook v0.6.0, run in go-notebook v0.18.0; on go-embedded-julia v0.20.0 since v0.21.2). go-embedded-julia is the pure-Go Julia these cells run on: its parser for the names and the syntax errors, its interpreter (v0.20.0) for the running. No external julia is started.

Running

The cells of a notebook share one Julia kernel, in the worker. A global, a function or a struct a cell defines is there in the next cell; what a cell prints is its own output, and the value of its last expression is shown as the Julia REPL shows it, unless it is nothing or the cell ends in a semicolon.

```julia
square(x) = x^2
total = sum(square(i) for i in 1:4)
```

```julia
println("total = ", total)
total + 1
```
$ notebook run julia.md
── cell 0 (line 4, ran in 1.102209s)
 30
── cell 1 (line 9, ran in 1.478ms)
 total = 30
 31

(A real transcript, from the change that became go-notebook v0.18.0, on an Apple M4 Max; the first cell pays the kernel’s cold start.)

An exception fails the cell with julia’s text of it after ERROR:, after the output the cell wrote before it; the cells that read it do not run, and the kernel keeps what it had.

The image. The kernel boots from go-embedded-julia’s prebuilt Base image, which is not part of the module. The first Julia cell a worker runs fetches the image of release v0.17.0 and loads it only if its SHA-256 is the one go-notebook pins (d243d2b748afb7d331227195d835357b6502184bedcdc4bcc296854276c2f6ec); the verified file is kept in your user cache directory (go-embedded-julia/images) and checked again each time. The fetch is bounded to five minutes and tried once. The cold start is about a second. On a machine that is offline and has no cached image every Julia cell of the run fails at once with the Julia kernel could not start, and the other cells run.

Limits. A notebook may come from anyone, so each cell is bounded, as an R cell is: 30 seconds, 50 million statements, a memory budget of 512 MiB, and 16 MiB of output per stream. The memory budget counts the elements of the arrays and dictionary tables a cell allocates, in total and garbage included, at 16 bytes each. It is a floor, not the heap: a boxed value costs more, strings are not counted, and one array may not have more than 2^24 elements whatever the budget. A cell over a limit is stopped and says which, in the kernel’s words; --timeout and --memory still apply to the worker. The kernel is sandboxed: its file system holds julia’s own tree and its environment is empty.

Soft scope. As in IJulia, a loop at the top level that updates a global works: s=0; for i in 1:10; s+=i; end gives 55. A MethodError shows Julia’s own text (no method matching, closest candidates).

Since go-notebook v0.21.0, a Float64 A * x runs through go-blas, a non-ASCII uppercase, lowercase or normalize works, and an n×0 matrix crosses.

Known limitations (go-embedded-julia v0.20.0):

  • A process loads one image release (#49).

Parsing and names

The names below are the same whether a cell runs or not.

Parsing. A Julia cell is parsed by go-embedded-julia’s port of JuliaSyntax, the parser julia 1.12 ships, which gives the same Expr trees as julia on its whole test corpus. A syntax error is reported at the notebook’s line and column, with julia’s own message:

```julia
y = 2
x = (1,
```
$ notebook run broken.md
── cell 0 (line 4, not run)
 error: 5:8: cell 0: syntax error: Expected `)` or `,`
notebook: 1 cell(s) failed

The parse is bounded — 4 MiB per cell, a nesting depth of 1000 — so a notebook from anyone cannot make it run long or exhaust memory; a cell over the limits fails with a message saying so.

Names. A Julia cell joins the rules of cells and the dependency graph: one definition per name, no assignment to another cell’s variable, a name starting with _ kept in its cell. Its names follow Julia’s own scope rules for an interactive context, as written in Scope of Variables (Julia manual, 1.12):

Construct In the notebook
x = 1, a, b = …, x::Int = 1, global x = 1 at the top level, or in if/begin there defines the variable
f(x) = …, function f … end, macro m … end (as @m) defines a function or macro
const C = …, struct S, abstract type, primitive type, module M defines a constant or type
using A, using A: x, y, import A.B, import A as B defines what it binds (A; x and y; B)
function, macro and struct bodies, let, do, ->, comprehensions and generators hard scopes: an assignment there makes a local
for, while, try at the top level soft scopes: an assignment there to an existing global assigns it (as in the REPL and IJulia); otherwise it makes a local of the loop
a name read before the cell assigns it, in any scope where no local binds it a use: the cell depends on the cell that defines it

These rules are checked against julia itself: 61 cells, from each kind of definition to keyword defaults, where bounds and nested generators, are lowered by julia 1.12.6 (through REPL.softscope, the soft-scope rule of the REPL), and the globals julia declares and reads are the names go-notebook finds.

Across languages. Since go-notebook v0.19.0, Julia variables cross with Go cells in both directions (Kernel.Get/Set), and Julia is no longer Isolated: a Go cell that reads a Julia name depends on the Julia cell. This breaks v0.18.0, where Julia variables stayed in Julia.

  • Types that cross: Int64, Float64 (bits kept, NaN payloads and -0.0 included), Bool, String, and Vector and Matrix of Float64 or Int64 (column-major). Go int and []int cross as Int64.
  • A Julia value of another type stays in Julia; the Go cell that reads it is deferred, naming the type.
  • A Go value Julia cannot take fails the Julia cell that reads it.
  • Inputs are measured before any copy: one array has at most 2^24 elements, and a cell’s inputs together are at most its memory limit. A cell can therefore hold up to twice its limit: its inputs plus its own allocations.

Between Julia cells every name is shared. The HTML page shows a Julia cell highlighted with go-rouge’s julia lexer.

In the browser

Since playground v0.18.0 the playground runs Julia cells (playground v0.21.0: go-embedded-julia v0.20.0) compiled to WebAssembly, with no external julia. It is the heaviest runtime the page has, so it is loaded on first use: a Julia cell’s badge reads Julia · loads when run (~28 MB), and Run downloads a third core (20 MB gzipped, the second core plus the interpreter) and the Base image (7.8 MB gzipped, checked against its pinned SHA-256 before it is decoded), then boots the kernel: about 28 MB and about 20 s the first time, shown on the cell as it loads, then cached by the browser. Opening a notebook, and running the cells above its first Julia cell, download nothing for Julia; the default, Ruby, R and Fortran cores never carry it. If the load fails (network, memory) the Julia cells say so and the other languages run.

  • Limits: 512 MiB of arrays, 20 million statements, 20 s (R’s is 10 s: a Julia cell compiles what it uses the first time) and 16 MiB of output. A cell that goes past one is stopped with a message that says which, and the worker is not killed. Deep recursion is a Julia StackOverflowError, not a lost core.
  • Julia is isolated from Go in the page. The variables that cross in notebook run (above) do not cross in the page, in either direction: a cell that reads one fails with the other language’s own message and a note saying why. Julia variables persist from one Julia cell to the next.
  • Each run starts from a reset kernel. Since playground v0.21.0, a run resets the kernel the page booted (Kernel.Reset, go-embedded-julia#93) instead of replacing the worker. A rerun takes 25 to 60 ms, and over 30 runs the page’s memory stays flat. The reset undoes what the earlier run changed, and it stops the tasks and timers that run started, so an @async loop or a periodic Timer never prints into the next run. A struct a notebook defines is not a redefinition the second time it runs. The worker is replaced only when a reset has to load the image again or fails.

Try the Julia example notebook.

item.title: R cells
item.description:
A ```r block is an R cell (parsed since go-notebook v0.8.0, run since v0.10.0). The R is go-embedded-r, a pure-Go R: go-notebook starts no external R. Its parser checks the cell and its evaluator runs it. Since v0.12.0 every R cell is bounded (see Limits). go-notebook v0.13.0 runs go-embedded-r v0.6.0: environments as values, the apply family and the string functions (v0.5.0), and regular expressions that follow R’s TRE (perl=TRUE and approximate matching are refused).

Since go-notebook v0.14.0 (go-embedded-r v0.13.1), a cell can use files and connections: readLines/writeLines, file.*, saveRDS/readRDS, source, sink/capture.output. The files live in a private in-memory file system of at most 64 MiB per notebook, shared by its R cells. No host file is reachable, and Sys.getenv sees no host variable: a notebook may come from anyone.

xs <- c(2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6)
total <- sum(xs)
total / length(xs)

Running

One environment. The R cells of a notebook share one global environment, so a variable assigned in one cell is there in the next, as in an R console. A cell re-runs only when it or an R cell it reads changes.

Output. What a cell prints is its output, as an R console shows it: print, cat, and the value of every visible top-level expression. An invisible value (x <- 1, invisible(x)) prints nothing. message() output and the cell’s warnings go to the standard error, the warnings in R’s own form (Warning message: then In f(x) : text; Warning messages: and a numbered line each when there are several). An error fails the cell as Error in f(x) : text, after the output written before it, and the cells that read it do not run. A cell that goes over a limit fails the same way.

A cell shows text only, no figure.

Limits

A notebook may come from anyone, so each R cell runs with its own bounds:

Limit Default Ends a cell with
memory 512 MiB of vectors allocated in total over the cell, garbage included Error: memory limit exceeded: more than 536870912 bytes of vectors allocated
steps (calls plus loop iterations) 50 million Error: evaluation step limit reached
time 30 s stopped: the R cell ran longer than 30s, the limit

The step count is measured: for (i in 1:n) s <- s + i stops at 16,666,666 iterations under 50 million steps, so a simulation of that size runs and an endless loop ends in seconds. The session and its variables survive a limit.

A program that embeds the kernel can change them with kernel.Options.R: a zero field is the default, and -1 is no bound. --timeout and --memory apply to R cells as to every cell, and they kill the worker, session included.

Parsing

An R cell is parsed by go-embedded-r’s port of R 4.6’s grammar, which gives the same trees and tokens as R 4.6.2 on all of R’s own src/library and tests (932 files). A syntax error is reported at the notebook’s line and column, with R’s own message:

```r
y <- 2
x <- y y
```
$ notebook run broken.md
── cell 0 (line 4, not run)
 error: 5:8: cell 0: syntax error: unexpected symbol
notebook: 1 cell(s) failed

The parse is bounded (4 MiB per cell, a nesting depth of 1000, a million nodes), so a notebook from anyone cannot make it run long or exhaust memory; a cell over the limits fails with a message saying so.

Names

An R cell joins the rules of cells and the dependency graph. Its names follow R’s scoping at the top level of the environment the cell runs in:

Construct In the notebook
x <- v, x = v, v -> x, "x" <- v defines x
assign("x", v) with a literal name defines x
x$a <- v, x[i] <- v, names(x) <- v defines x, and reads the x it modifies
for (i in s) at the top level defines i
f <- function(…) …, f = \(…) … at the top level defines the function f: it stays R’s
a free variable of the cell, or of a function’s body, that the cell does not assign a use: the cell depends on the cell that defines it
the parameters and local assignments of a function, and what local() assigns stay inside it

Dynamic cells. Some R cannot be analysed from its text: x <<- v, assign or get with a computed name, eval, parse, source, attach, library, require, environment<-. Such a cell is dynamic: it depends on every cell before it, and every later cell that reads a name depends on it, so nothing it may define is missed.

R variables stay in R. They are not shared with Go, Ruby, Julia or C cells in either direction yet: a Go cell that reads an R name finds it undefined, and an R cell does not see a Go variable.

In the browser

The playground does not run R cells: its WebAssembly cores do not link the evaluator. It parses and checks them: the + menu and the cell’s language menu offer R, its badge reads R · not runnable yet, a syntax error is shown at its line in R’s words, and the cells that read it are blocked, in the page’s neutral style and not as failures. Run the notebook with notebook run to execute its R cells.

item.title: Fortran cells
item.description:
A ```fortran block is a Fortran cell (checked since go-notebook v0.16.0, run since v0.17.0). The Fortran is go-embedded-fortran (v0.17.0), a pure-Go Fortran: no external compiler is started. Its sema session checks the cell and gives the names and the errors, its eval.Session runs it. A cell is a program’s loose material and units alike: declarations and statements at top level, subroutines, functions, modules, derived types, even a program. Free form, implicit typing off.

Cells share one session

A notebook with Fortran cells makes the worker import go-notebook’s fcells package, which owns one eval.Session. A Fortran cell sees the variables (with the values the earlier cells left), procedures, modules and derived types of the Fortran cells before it, in notebook order: n = n + 1 in a cell after the one that has integer :: n = 3 changes the same n. A cell with an error leaves nothing behind for the next ones. Names are case-insensitive. Redefinition shadows in Fortran (a cell that runs again defines a new version that later cells see); between two cells of the notebook it is refused, as go-notebook’s rule of one definition per name.

The names a cell reads from earlier Fortran cells are its uses and give the graph its edges: a variable, a procedure, a derived type named in a declaration and a module named in use all do.

Fortran variables stay in Fortran

They are not shared with Go, Ruby, Julia, R or C cells in either direction yet (analysis.Isolated, as R’s): a Go cell that reads a Fortran name finds it undefined, and a Fortran cell does not see a Go variable. A result reaches the reader as printed text; a cell shows text only.

Output and errors

What a cell prints is its output; standard error and the text of STOP are its standard error; STOP ends the cell, not the session. A refused cell or a failure is reported at line L, column C of the cell, and a cell that fails while it runs keeps what it had done.

Limits

A notebook may come from anyone. A cell may make at most 2^32 DO iterations and procedure calls, run 30 s, and the evaluator’s own bounds apply: 2^28 elements per array, 2^26 characters per string, 2^15 nested calls. Output is cut at 16 MiB per stream. The step count, not a timer, is what ends a loop in WebAssembly. --timeout and --memory apply as to every cell and kill the worker, session included. INCLUDE is refused: no file is read.

What the evaluator refuses

It says so, positioned: type extension and select type, pointer components, vector subscripts, elsewhere, dim= and mask=, complex variables, character arrays, read from a unit, and an array declared with an initialisation.

The playground

Fortran cells run in the browser playground, with no server and no compiler: the evaluator is linked into the playground’s second WebAssembly core (the one it loads for a notebook with a Fortran, R or Ruby cell; a Julia cell loads a third core that has it too), through fcells.Session.Eval; the default core stays Go-only. The playground bounds a cell tighter than the kernel does: 200 million DO iterations and procedure calls, 10 s and 16 MiB of output per stream. An endless do ends with step limit reached: the cell ran too many loop iterations and calls and the page stays usable. The second core grew by 1.3 MB (0.28 MB gzipped).

examples/fortran.md runs end to end: notebook run examples/fortran.md.

item.title: Adding a cell language
item.description:
A cell language is one registered implementation of analysis.Language, keyed by the first word of the fence’s info string. The graph, the kernel, the generator and the HTML export look a cell’s language up with analysis.Lookup and never test for a language by name. Go, Ruby, Julia and R are registered; a fence whose word is not registered stays prose.

type Language interface {
 Name() string // the fence word: "go", "ruby", "julia", ...
 Analyze(src string, lim Limits) (Names, []Diagnostic, error)
 Crosses(owner, user *Cell, name string) bool
 Run() Run
}

type Names struct {
 Defines, Uses []string
 Dynamic bool
}

The steps

  1. Implement Language and call analysis.Register from init. Analyze returns the names a cell defines and uses and its syntax errors (a Diagnostic carries a byte offset in the cell). It refuses a source over lim.MaxBytes, or nested deeper than lim.MaxDepth, with an error and never a panic.

  2. Say what crosses to other languages. Crosses(owner, user, name) is the owner’s rule for whether a cell of another language sees name. Within one language every name is shared. A Go cell sees a Ruby top-level local, not a Ruby method or constant; a language that cannot hold every name (Go keywords) implements NameChecker.

  3. Mark dynamic cells. Set Names.Dynamic when a cell’s names cannot be resolved statically: R’s <<-, assign and get with computed names, eval(parse()), attach, library(). The graph makes a dynamic cell depend on every earlier cell, and every later cell that reads any name depend on it, so it runs after anything before it changed and invalidates whatever may read what it defined.

  4. Say whether the cells run. Run{Runs: true} runs them. Otherwise the language is check-only: NotRun is the cell’s failure (C’s names its milestone M2), and Blocked, Reads and ReadsBlocked are the messages of the cells that read it, directly or through other cells.

  5. Optional capabilities, found by type assertion:

    Interface Gives
    CellAnalyzer the full Cell (chunks, funcs, types, display) instead of Names
    Highlighter the go-rouge lexer for the HTML export; without it the source is escaped
    Runtime the Go module the worker links (import path, module, default version); the kernel adds it to the work module
    TypeLearner variables typed when the cell has run, as Ruby’s

  6. Register the run backend for a language that runs, with gen.RegisterBackend(name, backend) from your own package. Infer declares the cell’s variables, Write writes its function and Runtime names the import and the prelude; the imported package comes from the language’s Runtime. The gen.Context it receives exposes the cell, its inputs, the declared variables and type resolution. No edit of gen is needed; Ruby’s backend (gen/ruby.go) is the model.

Testing

Test with a fake language that implements only Language, as analysis/lang_test.go does, and fuzz the dispatch with unknown or hostile fence words (FuzzDispatch). The project keeps 100 % coverage.
